topic.title: Equilibrium of a particle (including inclined planes)
topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 2 is one hour and fifty marks over six questions, sat every Summer. Equilibrium carries 6 to 8 marks a paper: a whole question when four forces act at a point, and the opening parts of the forces question otherwise. The reports call it a good differentiator, and the marks turn on whether a complete equation is written rather than on the arithmetic.
mustMemorise: In equilibrium the resultant is zero, so the total in each of two perpendicular directions is zero
At rest, held still and constant velocity all mean the forces balance
Every force with a part in a direction appears in that direction's equation
On a slope, resolve along the slope and at right angles to it
The normal reaction on a slope is mg cos of the slope's angle, always less than the weight
Friction holds a body still on a rough slope, acting up it and matching mg sin of the angle
notOnThisSpec: Limiting equilibrium, the coefficient of friction and F = μR: a frictional force is given, or is found from the balance itself
More than four separate forces, which the Teacher Guidance rules out
Equilibrium of a rigid body by moments: that is the uniform-rod topic, not this one
Lami's theorem and the triangle of forces
g = 9.8 m/s²: this unit takes g = 10 m/s², as the front page of every FM2 paper states

mustBeAbleTo: Say what equilibrium means: the resultant is zero and the acceleration is zero
Recognise at rest, held still and constant velocity as the same instruction
Choose two perpendicular directions and name each one in writing before resolving
Write a complete equation in each direction, with every force that has a part in it
Resolve along and at right angles to a slope, so only the weight needs splitting
Use friction as the force that holds a body still on a rough slope, acting up it
Find an unknown force or an unknown angle from the pair of equations
Round a final value to 2 decimal places when the question says so
sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, formula sheet on page 2. Equilibrium is examined as a whole question when four forces act at a point (Summer 2024 Q3: 3 marks for each of the two unknowns, and Summer 2026 Q2 in the same shape) and as the opening parts of a longer forces question otherwise (Summer 2023 Q3(i) and (ii), 2 marks each; Summer 2025 Q6(ii), 2 marks; Summer 2019 Q3(ii), 4 marks). The schemes give M for naming the direction and forming an equation, MW for the equation itself and W for the value, with follow-through into the later parts.
traps: Vertical equilibrium not recognised at all, so no equation is written (Summer 2019 Q3(ii))
An equation with two terms where three or four belong (Summer 2019 Q3(ii), Summer 2024 Q3)
The reaction written down as the weight, or as a single component, with no resolving (Summer 2023 Q3(i))
A zero acceleration not understood, so an acceleration is hunted for where the motion is steady (Summer 2023 Q3(ii))
One resolved component written down and nothing equated, so the later marks cannot be reached (Summer 2024 Q3)
Sine and cosine interchanged when resolving on a slope (Summer 2025 Q6(ii))

A block of mass $6$ kg rests on a rough horizontal table. A rope pulls the block with a force of $24$ N at $50°$ to the table, and the block does not move.

(i) Calculate the normal reaction of the table on the block.
(ii) Calculate the force due to friction. Round to 2 decimal places.

Because the reaction always equals the weight

workedExamples.stem:
A box of mass $14$ kg is held at rest on a smooth slope inclined at $27°$ to the horizontal by a rope lying along the slope.

(i) Calculate the tension in the rope.
(ii) Calculate the normal reaction of the slope on the box. Round to 2 decimal places.

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='300'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M26 270L366 96.8L366 270Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M72 270A46 46 0 0 0 67 249.1' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='80' y='262' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>27°</text><path d='M163.9 199.7L228.1 167L205.4 122.5L141.2 155.2Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='184.7' y='156.1' text-anchor='middle' font-size='14' font-weight='600'>14 kg</text><path d='M216.7 144.8L268.4 118.4' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M268.4 118.4L261.4 126.7L257.6 119.2Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='262' y='103.8' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>T</text><path d='M173.3 138.8L147 87.2' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M147 87.2L155.3 94.2L147.8 98Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='139' y='89.2' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>R</text><path d='M184.7 161.1L184.7 239.1' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M184.7 239.1L180.5 229.1L188.9 229.1Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='192.7' y='237.1' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>W</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: A box of mass 14 kg held at rest on a smooth slope inclined at 27 degrees. R leaves the box at right angles to the slope, its weight W points straight down, and T points up the slope along a rope.

steps.decision: Start by turning the mass into a force, as every equation that follows needs newtons.
Along the slope and at right angles to it is the pair worth choosing, because the tension and the reaction already lie along them and only the weight has to be split.

steps.working: Resolving at right angles to the slope: $R = 140\cos 27° = 124.74$ N.
steps.decision: The tension has no part at right angles to the slope, so this equation has just two terms in it.

options: Because the rope lies along the slope, so it is entirely in the other direction
Because the tension is too small to matter here
Because the reaction always balances the tension
whyMenu.explain: A force along one of the two chosen directions has no component in the other, which is exactly why that pair is chosen.

steps.working: Check: $124.74$ N is less than the weight of $140$ N, as it must be on a slope.
steps.decision: A reaction larger than the weight would mean the cosine of the angle was greater than one, so this check catches a swapped ratio.

workedExamples.stem:
A particle at $O$ is held in equilibrium by three forces: $20$ N acting horizontally to the right, $15$ N acting vertically downwards, and a force of $P$ N acting at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal, to the left.

(i) Calculate the value of $P$.
(ii) Calculate the value of $\theta$. Round to 2 decimal places.

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 330' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='330'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M100 165H300M200 65V265' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='0.9' stroke-dasharray='4 4' stroke-opacity='0.45'/><circle cx='200' cy='165' r='3.5' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M200 165L304 165' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M304 165L294 169.2L294 160.8Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='314' y='170' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>20 N</text><path d='M200 165L200 269' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M200 269L195.8 259L204.2 259Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='200' y='291' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>15 N</text><path d='M200 165L114.8 105.3' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M114.8 105.3L125.4 107.6L120.6 114.5Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='106.6' y='97.6' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>P N</text><path d='M168.9 143.2A38 38 0 0 0 162 165' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='148.5' y='153.8' text-anchor='end' font-size='14'>θ</text><text x='192' y='185' text-anchor='end' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>O</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: A particle at O held in equilibrium by three forces: 20 N horizontally to the right, 15 N vertically downwards, and a force of P newtons acting up and to the left at an angle theta to the horizontal.

steps.decision: The third force is the only one with an unknown direction, so write its two components as $P\cos\theta$ and $P\sin\theta$ and let the equations find them.
The second equation comes from the other direction. Two equations, two unknowns.
$P\cos\theta$ and $P\sin\theta$ are the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle whose longest side is $P$, so Pythagoras gives $P^2 = 20^2 + 15^2$.
Dividing the two equations removes $P$ instead, leaving the angle on its own.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: taking $g = 10$ m/s², what is the weight of a body of mass $20$ kg?

options.feedback: That is the mass with newtons written after it.
That divides by $g$ instead of multiplying.
That uses $g = 9.8$, which this unit does not.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a force $F$ acts at an angle $\theta$ to a line. What is its component along that line?

options.feedback: The line is beside the angle, so it takes the cosine.
That is the component at right angles to the line.
Tangent compares the two components with each other.
The whole force only lies along the line when the angle is zero.

items.skill: Prerequisite: the weight on a slope
items.stem: From an earlier topic: a body of weight $W$ rests on a slope inclined at $\alpha$. What is the component of $W$ acting down the slope?

options.feedback: Down the slope is opposite the slope's angle, so it takes the sine.
That is the component pressing into the slope.
The whole weight acts down the slope only when the slope is vertical.
That can be larger than the weight itself, which no component ever is.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: solve $R + 18 = 90$.

options.feedback: Taking 18 from both sides leaves $R = 72$.
That adds 18 instead of subtracting it.
That ignores the 18 altogether.
That divides rather than subtracts.

items.stem: A particle is in equilibrium under four forces. What is the resultant of the four forces?

options.feedback: Nothing is left over, which is exactly why the particle does not accelerate.
Every force takes part in the balance, so none of them survives on its own.

options.text: the total of the four sizes
options.feedback: That totals the sizes and ignores the directions, which is what makes them cancel.

options.text: it cannot be found without the mass
options.feedback: Equilibrium fixes the resultant at zero whatever the mass is.

items.stem: A crate is dragged across a floor at a constant velocity of $3$ m/s. What is true of the forces on it?

options.text: they balance, because the acceleration is zero
options.feedback: Constant velocity means no acceleration, so $F = ma$ gives a resultant of zero.

options.text: they do not balance, because the crate is moving
options.feedback: Motion at a steady speed needs nothing left over; it is changing speed that does.

options.text: the driving force must be larger than the friction
options.feedback: A larger driving force would speed the crate up, so the velocity would not be constant.

options.text: there is not enough information to say
options.feedback: Constant velocity is all the information needed: it sets the resultant to zero.

items.skill: The reaction when a rope lifts
items.stem: A block of weight $70$ N rests on a table while a rope pulls it with a vertical component of $20$ N upwards. Which equation gives the normal reaction?

options.feedback: The table and the rope together hold the weight up, so their totals match it.
That leaves the rope out. The reports describe candidates giving the reaction as the weight with no resolving done.
That leaves the weight out and keeps only the rope.
The rope pulls upwards, the same way as the reaction, so it takes work away from the table rather than adding to it.

items.stem: A box of weight $150$ N is held at rest on a smooth slope inclined at $30°$ to the horizontal by a rope parallel to the slope. What is the normal reaction?

options.feedback: Only the part of the weight pressing into the surface has to be balanced.
The reaction equals the weight only on a horizontal surface, where nothing else is vertical.
That is the component down the slope, which friction or a rope has to balance instead.
Tangent compares the two components and cannot give either from the weight.

items.skill: A component is not an equation
items.stem: A candidate resolving a force in an equilibrium question writes $25\sin 40°$ and stops. How is that marked?

options.text: a method mark for one correct resolved component, and no more
options.feedback: The schemes allow the first mark for a correct component; the marks after it are for the equation it belongs in.

options.text: full marks, because the resolving is right
options.feedback: The question asks for a value, and a value needs the complete equation.
A correct component is worth something, which is why it is always worth writing down.

options.text: a method mark only if the answer that follows is right
options.feedback: A method mark stands on its own, whatever comes after it.

items.stem: Three forces have vertical parts: a reaction $R$ upwards, a pull of $22\sin 36°$ upwards and a weight of $75$ N downwards. Which vertical equation is complete?

options.feedback: All three vertical parts appear, and the two upward ones together match the weight.
The weight has dropped out. This exact two-term shape is the one the reports single out.
The pull has dropped out, so the table is being asked to hold the whole weight.
The pull acts upwards, so it helps the reaction rather than adding to what it must support.

items.stem: A crate of weight $90$ N rests on a rough slope inclined at $25°$, with nothing attached to it. What is the force due to friction?

options.feedback: Friction is the only force along the slope, so it matches the component of the weight pulling the crate down it.
The size is right, but friction opposes the way the crate would slide, which is downwards.
That is the component pressing into the slope, which the normal reaction balances.
That is the whole weight. Only the part along the slope has to be held.

items.skill: Choosing the two directions on a slope
items.stem: Which pair of directions makes an equilibrium problem on a slope shortest to solve?

options.text: along the slope and at right angles to it
options.feedback: The reaction and any rope along the slope then need no resolving, leaving only the weight to split.
That works, but then both the reaction and the tension have to be resolved instead of one force.
That can be solved, but the two directions are not at right angles, so every force has to be resolved into both and the working grows.
Two different directions do give two equations, but unless they are at right angles each force has to be resolved awkwardly; perpendicular ones keep every equation short.

items.stem: A ring is held still by three strings pulling in different directions. Which statement must be true?

options.text: the forces on the ring have a resultant of zero
options.feedback: Held still means no acceleration, so nothing is left over: the forces cancel in every direction.
The strings pull in different directions, so they can balance with different sizes; nothing makes them equal.

options.text: the largest tension equals the total of the other two
options.feedback: That adds sizes as if the strings pulled along one line. They pull in different directions, so it is their parts that cancel.
The ring still has a weight; the upward parts of the tensions are what hold it up.

items.stem: A lift and its load weigh $7500$ N. The lift rises at a steady $2$ m/s. What is the tension in its cable?

options.feedback: A steady speed means no acceleration, so the forces balance: the cable holds exactly the weight.

options.text: more than $7500$ N, because the lift is rising
options.feedback: Rising at a steady speed needs nothing left over; a larger tension would make the lift speed up.
A smaller tension would leave a downward resultant, and the lift would slow down.

options.text: it cannot be found without the lift's mass
options.feedback: The weight is given, and a steady speed sets the resultant to zero: that is all the equation needs.

context.setting: A crate held on a smooth ramp

parts.stem:
A crate of mass $12$ kg is held at rest on a smooth ramp inclined at $20°$ to the horizontal by a rope lying along the ramp.

Calculate the tension in the rope. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: Work out the weight first.
Resolve along the ramp.
parts.workedSolution: Weight $= 12 \times 10 = 120$ N. Resolving along the ramp, $T = 120\sin 20° = 41.04$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $120\cos 20°$, the component pressing into the ramp. Along the ramp is opposite the angle, so it takes the sine.
That is the whole weight. Only the part of it acting along the ramp has to be held by the rope.

parts.stem:
Calculate the normal reaction of the ramp on the crate. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: resolving at right angles to the ramp: $R = 120\cos 20°$

hints: The rope lies along the ramp, so it has no part at right angles to it.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving at right angles to the ramp, $R = 120\cos 20° = 112.76$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the reaction on a horizontal surface. On a ramp only part of the weight presses into the surface, so the reaction is smaller.
That is the component along the ramp, which the rope holds. Into the ramp sits beside the angle and takes the cosine.

questions.solutionProgram: W = 12 * 10; T = W * sin(20 deg); R = W * cos(20 deg)

context.setting: A body at rest under several forces

parts.stem:
A particle rests in equilibrium under four forces.

State what this tells you about the resultant of the forces, and about the acceleration of the particle.

accepted: The resultant is zero, so the acceleration is zero.
The resultant of the forces is zero and the acceleration is zero.

any: resultant of the forces is zero

hints: What is left over when forces cancel?
parts.workedSolution: The resultant is zero, and since $F = ma$ with no resultant force, the acceleration is zero as well.

commonErrors.feedback: Describing the motion is not the same as describing the forces. Equilibrium is a statement about the resultant, and it holds at a steady speed just as it does at rest.

parts.stem:
A crate of mass $11$ kg rests on a rough slope inclined at $16°$ to the horizontal, with nothing attached to it.

Calculate the force due to friction on the crate. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: Which force is the only one lying along the slope?
The crate is at rest, so the forces along the slope balance.
parts.workedSolution: The crate is at rest, so resolving along the slope, $F = 110\sin 16° = 30.32$ N, acting up the slope.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $110\cos 16°$, which is what the normal reaction balances. Friction lies along the slope and takes the sine.
That is the whole weight. Friction only has to balance the part of it that pulls the crate down the slope.

parts.stem:
Calculate the normal reaction of the slope on the crate. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: resolving at right angles to the slope: $R = 110\cos 16°$

hints: Friction lies along the slope, so it has no part at right angles to it.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving at right angles to the slope, $R = 110\cos 16° = 105.74$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That gives the reaction the whole weight to balance, which only happens on a horizontal surface.

questions.solutionProgram: W = 11 * 10; F = W * sin(16 deg); R = W * cos(16 deg)

parts.stem:
A block of weight $80$ N is pulled along a rough horizontal table at a constant velocity by a rope. The pull along the rope is $50$ N and the rope makes an angle of $30°$ with the table.

Calculate the normal reaction of the table on the block. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: resolving vertically, with all three vertical forces named

hints: Three forces have a vertical part.
The rope pulls partly upwards.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving vertically: $R + 50\sin 30° = 80$, so $R = 80 - 25 = 55$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That leaves the rope out of the vertical equation. Part of the pull is upwards, so the table has less to support.
The resolved component is right, so the first method mark (M) stands, but the rope pulls upwards, so it takes weight off the table rather than adding to it.
That uses $50\cos 30°$, the part of the pull along the table. The vertical part is opposite the angle and takes the sine.

parts.stem:
Calculate the force due to friction on the block. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: Constant velocity means the horizontal forces balance too.
parts.workedSolution: The velocity is constant, so resolving horizontally, $F = 50\cos 30° = 43.30$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $50\sin 30°$, the vertical part of the pull. Along the table sits beside the angle and takes the cosine.
That is the whole pull. The rope is at an angle, so only part of it drags the block along the table.

questions.solutionProgram: R = 80 - 50 * sin(30 deg); F = 50 * cos(30 deg)

context.setting: Three forces holding a particle still

parts.stem:
A particle is held in equilibrium by three forces. One is $12$ N acting horizontally to the right and another is $5$ N acting vertically upwards.

Calculate the magnitude of the third force.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: the third force recognised as equal and opposite to the resultant of the other two

hints: What must the third force cancel?
The first two act at right angles.
parts.workedSolution: The three forces total zero, so the third must balance the other two. Their resultant has magnitude $\sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = 13$ N, so the third force is $13$ N in the opposite direction.

commonErrors.feedback: That totals the two sizes. They act at right angles, so the force that balances them is shorter than their sum.
That is the sum of the squares, so the method marks (M) stand. The square root finishes it.

figures.alt: Four forces acting at a point O in equilibrium: 26 N up and to the right at 40 degrees to the vertical, 18 N down and to the right at 19 degrees to the horizontal, P newtons horizontally to the left, and W newtons vertically downwards.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows four forces holding the point $O$ in equilibrium: $P$ N horizontally to the left, $W$ N vertically downwards, $26$ N up and to the right at $40°$ to the vertical, and $18$ N down and to the right at $19°$ below the horizontal.

Calculate the value of $W$. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: resolving vertically and equating the totals

hints: Three of the four forces have a vertical part.
The angle of the 26 N force is measured from the vertical.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving vertically: $26\cos 40° = W + 18\sin 19°$, so $W = 19.92 - 5.86 = 14.06$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is a two-term equation, $W = 26\cos 40°$, with the $18$ N force left out. Its vertical part acts downwards as well, so it belongs in the balance.
Resolving vertically and equating earns the method mark (M), but the $18$ N force pulls downwards, the same way as $W$, so it is on the same side of the equation.
Both ratios are the wrong way round: the $40°$ is measured from the vertical, so the vertical part takes the cosine, and the $19°$ is from the horizontal, so its vertical part takes the sine.

parts.stem:
Calculate the value of $P$. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: resolving horizontally and equating the totals

hints: Three of the four forces have a horizontal part.
Both angled forces push the same way horizontally.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving horizontally: $P = 26\sin 40° + 18\cos 19° = 16.71 + 17.02 = 33.73$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That leaves the $26$ N force out of the horizontal equation. Its horizontal part pushes the same way, so both belong.
Both ratios are swapped. The $40°$ is measured from the vertical, so the horizontal part takes the sine; the $19°$ is from the horizontal, so its horizontal part takes the cosine.
Resolving horizontally and equating earns the method mark (M), but the two angled forces push the same way, so their horizontal parts add rather than cancel.
That leaves the $18$ N force out of the horizontal equation. Its horizontal part pushes the same way as the $26$ N force's, so both belong.

questions.solutionProgram: W = 26 * cos(40 deg) - 18 * sin(19 deg); P = 26 * sin(40 deg) + 18 * cos(19 deg)

parts.stem:
A box of mass $9$ kg is dragged across a rough horizontal table at a constant velocity by a rope. The pull along the rope is $38$ N and the rope makes an angle of $24°$ with the table.

State what the constant velocity tells you about the acceleration of the box, and about the forces on it.

accepted: The acceleration is zero, so the forces balance.
There is no acceleration, so the resultant force is zero.

scheme.for: so the forces balance in both directions

hints: A velocity that does not change is an acceleration of what?
parts.workedSolution: A constant velocity means the acceleration is zero, so by $F = ma$ the resultant force is zero and the forces balance in both directions.

commonErrors.feedback: A steady speed is not a changing one. With nothing left over the box keeps the speed it has, which is what constant velocity means.

parts.stem:
Calculate the normal reaction of the table on the box. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: resolving vertically with all three vertical forces named

hints: Work out the weight first.
The rope pulls partly upwards.
parts.workedSolution: Weight $= 9 \times 10 = 90$ N. Resolving vertically: $R + 38\sin 24° = 90$, so $R = 74.54$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the reaction with the rope ignored. Part of the pull is upwards, so the table supports less than the whole weight.
The resolved component is right, so the method mark (M) stands, but the rope pulls upwards, so its part is taken away from the weight, not added to it.
That uses $38\cos 24°$, the part of the pull along the table. The vertical part is opposite the angle and takes the sine.

parts.stem:
Calculate the force due to friction on the box. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: resolving horizontally and equating the totals

hints: The velocity is constant, so the horizontal forces balance.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving horizontally: $F = 38\cos 24° = 34.71$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $38\sin 24°$, the vertical part of the pull. Along the table sits beside the angle and takes the cosine.
That is the whole pull along the rope. Only the part of it that lies along the table has to be balanced by friction.

questions.solutionProgram: W = 9 * 10; R = W - 38 * sin(24 deg); F = 38 * cos(24 deg)

hints: Turn the mass into a weight first.
Along the slope is opposite the slope's angle.
parts.workedSolution: Weight $= 15 \times 10 = 150$ N. Resolving along the slope: $T = 150\sin 32° = 79.49$ N.

parts.stem:

hints: The rope lies along the slope, so it has no part at right angles to it.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving at right angles to the slope: $R = 150\cos 32° = 127.21$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That gives the reaction the whole weight to balance, which happens only on a horizontal surface.
That is the component along the slope, which the rope holds. Into the slope takes the cosine.

figures.alt: A particle at O held in equilibrium by three forces: 45 N horizontally to the right, 28 N vertically downwards, and a force of P newtons acting up and to the left at an angle theta to the horizontal that has to be found.

parts.stem:
A particle at $O$ is held in equilibrium by three forces. A force of $45$ N acts horizontally to the right and a force of $28$ N acts vertically downwards. The third force, of $P$ N, acts at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal, to the left.

Calculate the value of $P$.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: resolving horizontally and equating the totals

hints: Write the unknown force's two components as $P\cos\theta$ and $P\sin\theta$.
The two components are the shorter sides of a right-angled triangle with $P$ as its longest side.
parts.workedSolution: Horizontally: $P\cos\theta = 45$. Vertically: $P\sin\theta = 28$. These are the shorter sides of a right-angled triangle with longest side $P$, so by Pythagoras $P^2 = 45^2 + 28^2 = 2809$ and $P = 53$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That totals the two sizes. They act at right angles, so the force that balances them comes from Pythagoras instead.
That is $P^2$, so all three method marks (M) are safe. The square root is the last step.

parts.stem:
Calculate the value of $\theta$. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ °

scheme.for: the two equations divided, or one of them used with the value of $P$

hints: Dividing the two equations removes $P$.
parts.workedSolution: Dividing the vertical equation by the horizontal one, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{28}{45}$, so $\theta = 31.89°$.

commonErrors.feedback: That fraction is the wrong way up and gives the angle with the vertical. The question measures $\theta$ from the horizontal.
That is the size of the force from part (a), not an angle. The angle comes from the ratio of the two components.

figures.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 330' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='330'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M100 165H300M200 65V265' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='0.9' stroke-dasharray='4 4' stroke-opacity='0.45'/><circle cx='200' cy='165' r='3.5' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M200 165L266.8 85.3' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M266.8 85.3L263.6 95.7L257.2 90.3Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='273.3' y='75.7' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>36 N</text><path d='M224.4 135.9A38 38 0 0 0 200 127' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='218.5' y='119.3' text-anchor='start' font-size='14'>40°</text><path d='M200 165L96 165' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M96 165L106 160.8L106 169.2Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='86' y='170' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>P N</text><path d='M200 165L200 269' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M200 269L195.8 259L204.2 259Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='200' y='291' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>W N</text><text x='192' y='185' text-anchor='end' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>O</text></g></svg>
figures.alt: Three forces at a point O in equilibrium: 36 N up and to the right at 40 degrees to the vertical, P newtons horizontally to the left, and W newtons vertically downwards.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows three forces on a particle at $O$: a force of $36$ N at $40°$ to the vertical, a horizontal force of $P$ N and a vertical force of $W$ N. The forces are in equilibrium.

Calculate the value of $P$. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: The angle is measured from the vertical. Which side of the triangle is next to it?
The horizontal part is the side opposite the angle.
parts.workedSolution: The angle is measured from the vertical, so the horizontal part of the 36 N force is opposite it and takes the sine. Resolving horizontally, $P = 36\sin 40° = 23.14$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $36\cos 40°$, the vertical part. Measured from the vertical, the side next to the angle is vertical, so the horizontal part takes the sine.
That is the whole 36 N force. It acts at an angle, so only its horizontal part balances $P$.
That is $40\sin 36°$: the size of the force and its angle have changed places. The force is 36 N and the angle 40°.

parts.stem:
Calculate the value of $W$. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: Only two forces have a vertical part: the angled force and W.
parts.workedSolution: The vertical part of the 36 N force is next to the angle, so it takes the cosine. Resolving vertically, $W = 36\cos 40° = 27.58$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $36\sin 40°$, the horizontal part from part (a). The vertical side is next to an angle measured from the vertical, so it takes the cosine.
That is the whole 36 N force. Only its vertical part holds up $W$.

questions.solutionProgram: P = 36 * sin(40 deg); W = 36 * cos(40 deg)

context.setting: A crate held on a rough slope by a rope and friction together

figures.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='300'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M26 270L366 73.7L366 270Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M72 270A46 46 0 0 0 65.8 247' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='80' y='262' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>30°</text><path d='M164.8 189.9L227.2 153.9L202.2 110.5L139.8 146.5Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='183.5' y='145.2' text-anchor='middle' font-size='14' font-weight='600'>8 kg</text><path d='M214.7 132.2L264.9 103.2' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M264.9 103.2L258.3 111.8L254.1 104.6Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='257.4' y='89.1' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>25 N</text></g></svg>
figures.alt: A crate of mass 8 kg at rest on a rough slope inclined at 30 degrees, pulled up the slope by a rope parallel to it with a force of 25 N.

parts.stem:
A crate of mass $8$ kg rests on a rough slope inclined at $30°$ to the horizontal. A rope parallel to the slope pulls the crate up the slope with a force of $25$ N, and the crate stays at rest.

Calculate the size of the force due to friction.

Answer ________ N
hints: Work out the part of the weight acting down the slope first.
The rope and friction together hold that part.
parts.workedSolution: The weight is $8 \times 10 = 80$ N, and its part down the slope is $80\sin 30° = 40$ N. The rope holds 25 N of it, so friction holds the rest: $25 + F = 40$ and $F = 15$ N, up the slope.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the whole of the weight's part down the slope, as if friction held the crate alone. The 25 N rope belongs in the equation too.
That adds the rope's 25 N to the weight's part, but the rope pulls up the slope, the same way as friction, so it takes work away from friction rather than adding to it.
That uses $80\cos 30°$, the part pressing into the slope. Down the slope is opposite the slope's angle, so it takes the sine.

parts.stem:
Calculate the normal reaction of the slope on the crate. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: resolving at right angles to the slope: $R = 80\cos 30°$

hints: The rope and friction both lie along the slope, so neither has a part at right angles to it.
parts.workedSolution: Only the weight has a part at right angles to the slope. Resolving that way, $R = 80\cos 30° = 69.28$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the reaction on a level floor. On a slope only part of the weight presses into the surface.
That is $80\sin 30°$, the part down the slope. Into the slope is next to the angle, so it takes the cosine.

parts.stem:
The pull in the rope is increased to $50$ N, and the crate still does not move.

In which direction does the force due to friction now act on the crate?

options.feedback: The rope now pulls up with 50 N, more than the weight's 40 N part down the slope, so the crate would slide up: friction opposes that and acts down the slope, with 10 N.
Friction acts against the way the crate would slide. With 50 N up and only 40 N down, it would slide up, so friction points down the slope.
The two forces along the slope do not match (50 N against 40 N), so something must make up the difference: friction, down the slope.

hints: Compare the rope's pull with the weight's part down the slope. Which way would the crate slide without friction?
parts.workedSolution: Without friction the crate would slide up, because 50 N up the slope is more than the weight's 40 N part down it. Friction opposes that, so it acts down the slope.

questions.solutionProgram: W = 8 * 10; F = W * sin(30 deg) - 25; R = W * cos(30 deg); with 50 N: F = 50 - W * sin(30 deg), down the slope

context.setting: Four forces at a point, with angles to the vertical and to the horizontal

figures.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 330' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='330'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M100 165H300M200 65V265' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='0.9' stroke-dasharray='4 4' stroke-opacity='0.45'/><circle cx='200' cy='165' r='3.5' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M200 165L140.3 250.2' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M140.3 250.2L142.6 239.6L149.5 244.4Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='134.6' y='270.4' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>40 N</text><path d='M178.2 196.1A38 38 0 0 0 200 203' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='183.8' y='221.5' text-anchor='end' font-size='14'>35°</text><path d='M200 165L297.7 129.4' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M297.7 129.4L289.8 136.8L286.9 128.9Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='307.1' y='124' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>34 N</text><path d='M238 165A38 38 0 0 0 235.7 152' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='253.2' y='160.6' text-anchor='start' font-size='14'>20°</text><path d='M200 165L96 165' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M96 165L106 160.8L106 169.2Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='86' y='170' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>P N</text><path d='M200 165L200 61' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M200 61L204.2 71L195.8 71Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='200' y='49' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>Q N</text></g></svg>
figures.alt: Four forces at a point in equilibrium: 40 N down and to the left at 35 degrees to the vertical, 34 N up and to the right at 20 degrees above the horizontal, P newtons horizontally to the left, and Q newtons vertically upwards.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows four forces on a particle. A force of $40$ N acts at $35°$ to the vertical, a force of $34$ N acts at $20°$ to the horizontal, a force of $P$ N acts horizontally and a force of $Q$ N acts vertically upwards. The forces are in equilibrium.

Calculate the value of $Q$. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: resolving vertically, with both angled forces resolved

hints: Three forces have a vertical part. Which two point up?
The 40 N angle is from the vertical, so its vertical part takes the cosine.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving vertically, the upward parts match the downward one: $Q + 34\sin 20° = 40\cos 35°$, so $Q + 11.63 = 32.77$ and $Q = 21.14$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That leaves the 34 N force out, but it has an upward part, $34\sin 20°$, which helps $Q$ hold the particle up.
That takes $40\sin 35°$ for the vertical part, but the 35° is measured from the vertical, so the vertical side is next to it and takes the cosine.
That adds the 34 N force's vertical part to the downward one, but it points up, the same way as $Q$, so it reduces what $Q$ has to hold.

parts.stem:
Calculate the value of $P$. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: resolving horizontally, with both angled forces resolved

hints: P and the 40 N force both have parts to the left; the 34 N force's part is to the right.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving horizontally, the parts to the left match the part to the right: $P + 40\sin 35° = 34\cos 20°$, so $P + 22.94 = 31.95$ and $P = 9.01$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That leaves the 40 N force out, but it has a horizontal part, $40\sin 35°$, to the left, alongside $P$.
That uses the whole 34 N, but it acts at 20° to the horizontal, so only $34\cos 20°$ of it is horizontal.
That adds the 40 N force's horizontal part to the 34 N force's, but they point opposite ways, so one is taken from the other.

parts.stem:
The forces $P$ and $Q$ are replaced by a single force that keeps the particle in equilibrium.

Calculate the magnitude of this single force. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: Pythagoras on the values of $P$ and $Q$

hints: The single force must do the work of P and Q together: they are its two parts.
parts.workedSolution: $P$ and $Q$ are at right angles, so they are the two parts of the single force: $\sqrt{9.01^2 + 21.14^2} = 22.98$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That adds $P$ and $Q$ as if they pointed the same way. They are at right angles, so the single force comes from Pythagoras.
That is $P^2 + Q^2$. The square root is the last step of Pythagoras.

questions.solutionProgram: Q = 40 * cos(35 deg) - 34 * sin(20 deg); P = 34 * cos(20 deg) - 40 * sin(35 deg); S = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2)

context.setting: A crate pushed at a steady speed, then harder

parts.stem:
A crate of mass $20$ kg is pushed across a rough floor by a horizontal force. With a push of $60$ N the crate moves at a constant velocity.

Write down the resistance to the crate's motion.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: $60$ N: at constant velocity the forces balance

hints: Constant velocity: what does that say about the acceleration, and so about the forces?
parts.workedSolution: Constant velocity means no acceleration, so the forces balance: the resistance equals the push, 60 N.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides the push by the mass, looking for an acceleration where there is none. Constant velocity means the forces balance, so the resistance equals the push.

parts.stem:
The push is increased to $90$ N. The resistance to motion does not change.

Calculate the acceleration of the crate.

Answer ________ m/s²
hints: The forces no longer balance. What is left over?
Then use F = ma with the mass, not the weight.
parts.workedSolution: The forces no longer balance: the resultant is $90 - 60 = 30$ N forwards. By $F = ma$, $30 = 20a$, so $a = 1.5$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That uses the whole 90 N push, but the 60 N resistance still acts against it. $F$ in $F = ma$ is the resultant.
That divides by the weight, 200 N. In $F = ma$ the $m$ is the mass, 20 kg.
That adds the resistance to the push, but it acts backwards, so it is taken away.

findTheMistake.stem: Eoin is finding the normal reaction on a block of weight $75$ N resting on a rough table. A rope pulls the block at $36°$ to the table with a force of $22$ N, and the block does not move. His working:
studentWorking: the block does not move, so the vertical forces balance
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 has only two terms where three belong. Three forces have a vertical part: the reaction upwards, the rope's $22\sin 36°$ upwards, and the weight of $75$ N downwards. Leaving the weight out makes the equation say the rope alone is being balanced.
findTheMistake.feedback: Naming the direction and saying the forces balance is the method, and it earns the method mark (M). Before writing an equation, list every force that has a part in that direction: three here, so three terms. The examiners describe the two-term equation as very common in this kind of question.

findTheMistake.stem: Aoife is finding the normal reaction on a box of mass $11$ kg held at rest on a smooth slope inclined at $24°$ by a rope parallel to the slope. Her working:
studentWorking: the box is at rest, so the reaction balances the weight
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 skips the resolving. The reaction is at right angles to the slope and the weight is vertical, so they are not in the same direction and cannot simply match. Only the component of the weight pressing into the slope, $110\cos 24°$, is balanced by $R$.
correction: resolving at right angles to the slope: $R = 110\cos 24°$
findTheMistake.feedback: Turning the mass into a weight is worth the first mark, and it is right here. Two forces balance only when they lie along the same line: check that before equating anything, and on a slope the reaction and the weight never do.

findTheMistake.stem: Dara is working with a crate that is being dragged across a floor at a constant velocity of $4$ m/s. His working:
studentWorking: the crate is moving, so the forces do not balance
the pull must be larger than the friction
so there is a resultant force and the crate accelerates
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 reads movement as a sign of a resultant force. What creates a resultant is a change of velocity, not velocity itself. The velocity here is constant, so the acceleration is zero and the forces do balance.
correction: the velocity is constant, so the acceleration is zero
$F = ma$ with $a = 0$ gives a resultant of zero
so the pull along the floor and the friction are equal
findTheMistake.feedback: Nothing here can be credited yet, because the first line sets the whole method off in the wrong direction. Read the words for the acceleration, not the motion: at rest, held still and constant velocity all mean the same thing, and all three mean the forces balance.

prompts.prompt: What does it mean for a particle to be in equilibrium?
prompts.answer: The resultant of the forces on it is zero, so it has no acceleration.

prompts.prompt: How many equations does an equilibrium problem give you, and where do they come from?
prompts.answer: Two, one from each of two perpendicular directions, with the total in each set to zero.

prompts.prompt: A candidate writes one correct resolved component and stops. What is still needed?
prompts.answer: An equation with every force that has a part in that direction, set equal to zero.

prompts.prompt: Which three phrases in a question all mean the forces balance?
prompts.answer: At rest, held still, and moving with constant velocity.

prompts.prompt: Which two directions make an equilibrium problem on a slope shortest?
prompts.answer: Along the slope and at right angles to it, because only the weight then needs resolving.

prompts.prompt: A box of weight W rests on a slope inclined at an angle. What is the normal reaction?
prompts.answer: W cosine of the angle, because only that component of the weight presses into the surface.

prompts.prompt: Why is the normal reaction not equal to the weight when a rope pulls a block at an angle?
prompts.answer: Part of the pull is upwards, so the table supports less than the whole weight.

prompts.prompt: A crate rests on a rough slope with nothing attached. Which force holds it there?
prompts.answer: The force due to friction, acting up the slope.

prompts.prompt: What is the commonest shape of a wrong equilibrium equation?
prompts.answer: One with two terms where three or four belong, because a force has been left out.

prompts.prompt: Three forces hold a particle still and two of them are perpendicular. How do you find the third?
prompts.answer: It balances the resultant of the other two, so its magnitude comes from Pythagoras and its direction is opposite.

The papers give 3 marks to each half of a four-force equilibrium question (Summer 2024 Q3(i) and (ii)), 2 to a normal reaction on the flat or on a slope (Summer 2023 Q3(i), Summer 2025 Q6(ii)) and 4 to the vertical-equilibrium part of a longer question (Summer 2019 Q3(ii)). The four exam-style questions here are 6, 8, 8 and 7 marks. Time allowance is marks x 1.2 minutes.

checks.tool: claude (author-unit-batch pass; every value computed in scratchpad/fm2-batch-c before writing)
checks.detail: Every value is produced by the balance route on the stem's own numbers. Exam A: W = 26 cos 40 - 18 sin 19 = 14.0569287409 printed as 14.06; P = 26 sin 40 + 18 cos 19 = 33.7318122126 printed as 33.73; from the components rounded to 2 d.p. both come out the same to 2 d.p. Exam B: weight 90, R = 90 - 38 sin 24 = 74.5440075631 printed as 74.54, F = 38 cos 24 = 34.7147273904 printed as 34.71. Exam C: weight 150, T = 150 sin 32 = 79.487889635 printed as 79.49, R = 150 cos 32 = 127.207214423 printed as 127.21. Exam D: P = sqrt(2025 + 784) = 53, theta = 31.8907918018 printed as 31.89. Practice: 120 sin 20 = 41.04 and 120 cos 20 = 112.76; 110 sin 16 = 30.32 and 110 cos 16 = 105.74; 80 - 50 sin 30 = 55 and 50 cos 30 = 43.3; sqrt(144 + 25) = 13; 160 cos 35 = 131.06. The note's own examples: 140 sin 27 = 63.56, 140 cos 27 = 124.74, 70 sin 18 = 21.63, 70 cos 18 = 66.57, and 20 N with 15 N giving 25 N at 36.87°. Twins: 90 - 40 sin 35 = 67.06, 130 sin 22 = 48.7, sqrt(225 + 64) = 17. Every distractor is produced by executing a wrongly shaped balance (a term dropped, a sign kept, a ratio swapped, a force left unresolved) through the same route, and re-checked against the published JSON by verify-published.mjs.

Exam B: weight 90, R = 90 - 38 sin 24 = 74.5440075631 printed as 74.54, F = 38 cos 24 = 34.7147273904 printed as 34.71. The note's own examples: 140 sin 27 = 63.56, 140 cos 27 = 124.74, 70 sin 18 = 21.63, 70 cos 18 = 66.57, and 20 N with 15 N giving 25 N at 36.87°. Twins: 90 - 40 sin 35 = 67.06, 130 sin 22 = 48.7, sqrt(225 + 64) = 17. Every distractor is produced by executing a wrongly shaped balance (a term dropped, a sign kept, a ratio swapped, a force left unresolved) through the same route, and re-checked against the published JSON by verify-published.mjs.

checks.detail: Every value is produced by the balance route on the stem's own numbers. Exam A: W = 26 cos 40 - 18 sin 19 = 14.0569287409 printed as 14.06; P = 26 sin 40 + 18 cos 19 = 33.7318122126 printed as 33.73; from the components rounded to 2 d.p. both come out the same to 2 d.p. Exam B: weight 90, R = 90 - 38 sin 24 = 74.5440075631 printed as 74.54, F = 38 cos 24 = 34.7147273904 printed as 34.71. Exam C: weight 150, T = 150 sin 32 = 79.487889635 printed as 79.49, R = 150 cos 32 = 127.207214423 printed as 127.21. Exam D: P = sqrt(2025 + 784) = 53, theta = 31.8907918018 printed as 31.89. Practice: 120 sin 20 = 41.04 and 120 cos 20 = 112.76; 110 sin 16 = 30.32 and 110 cos 16 = 105.74; 80 - 50 sin 30 = 55 and 50 cos 30 = 43.3; sqrt(144 + 25) = 13; 160 cos 35 = 131.06. The note's own examples: 140 sin 27 = 63.56, 140 cos 27 = 124.74, 70 sin 18 = 21.63, 70 cos 18 = 66.57, and 20 N with 15 N giving 25 N at 36.87°. Twins: 90 - 40 sin 35 = 67.06, 130 sin 22 = 48.7, sqrt(225 + 64) = 17. Every distractor is produced by executing a wrongly shaped balance (a term dropped, a sign kept, a ratio swapped, a force left unresolved) through the same route, and re-checked against the published JSON by verify-published.mjs.

A particle in equilibrium under up to four forces, as the Teacher Guidance limits: on the flat, on a smooth inclined plane and on a rough one where friction is the force that holds the body still, with an unknown force or an unknown angle found from two component equations. No coefficient of friction, no limiting equilibrium, no moments (those belong to the uniform-rod topic) and no three-dimensional work.

checks.detail: packs/further-maths/exam-true/tariffs.json FM2: per-question median 8 marks and 90th percentile 13; per-part median 2 and 90th percentile 4. The papers give 3 marks to each half of a four-force equilibrium question (Summer 2024 Q3(i) and (ii)), 2 to a normal reaction on the flat or on a slope (Summer 2023 Q3(i), Summer 2025 Q6(ii)) and 4 to the vertical-equilibrium part of a longer question (Summer 2019 Q3(ii)). The four exam-style questions here are 6, 8, 8 and 7 marks. Time allowance is marks x 1.2 minutes.

checks.tool: claude (author-unit-batch pass; every value computed in scratchpad/fm2-batch-c before writing)
checks.detail: Every value is produced by the balance route on the stem's own numbers. Exam A: W = 26 cos 40 - 18 sin 19 = 14.0569287409 printed as 14.06; P = 26 sin 40 + 18 cos 19 = 33.7318122126 printed as 33.73; from the components rounded to 2 d.p. both come out the same to 2 d.p. Exam B: weight 90, R = 90 - 38 sin 24 = 74.5440075631 printed as 74.54, F = 38 cos 24 = 34.7147273904 printed as 34.71. Exam C: weight 150, T = 150 sin 32 = 79.487889635 printed as 79.49, R = 150 cos 32 = 127.207214423 printed as 127.21. Exam D: P = sqrt(2025 + 784) = 53, theta = 31.8907918018 printed as 31.89. Practice: 120 sin 20 = 41.04 and 120 cos 20 = 112.76; 110 sin 16 = 30.32 and 110 cos 16 = 105.74; 80 - 50 sin 30 = 55 and 50 cos 30 = 43.3; sqrt(144 + 25) = 13; 160 cos 35 = 131.06. The note's own examples: 140 sin 27 = 63.56, 140 cos 27 = 124.74, 70 sin 18 = 21.63, 70 cos 18 = 66.57, and 20 N with 15 N giving 25 N at 36.87°. Twins: 90 - 40 sin 35 = 67.06, 130 sin 22 = 48.7, sqrt(225 + 64) = 17. Every distractor is produced by executing a wrongly shaped balance (a term dropped, a sign kept, a ratio swapped, a force left unresolved) through the same route, and re-checked against the published JSON by verify-published.mjs.
